milestones.claim: Quantinuum upgraded H2 to 56 qubits and ran random circuit sampling on it; the peer-reviewed paper reports 99.843(5)% two-qubit gate fidelity and states H2 can yield data “well beyond the reach of state-of-the art classical simulation methods”.

evidence.quote: Here, we describe recent hardware upgrades to Quantinuum’s H2 quantum computer, enabling it to operate on up to 56 qubits with arbitrary connectivity and 99.843(5)% two-qubit gate fidelity.
indicates that H2 can yield data well beyond the reach of state-of-the art classical simulation methods at unprecedented fidelities
A joint team from Quantinuum and JPMorgan Chase ran a Random Circuit Sampling (RCS) algorithm

milestones.claim: Quantinuum and Microsoft report entangled encoded qubits in the [[7,1,3]] and [[12,2,4]] codes on the 32-qubit H2 with error rates below physical levels, and state they created four “logical qubits” using 30 of the 32 physical qubits.

evidence.quote: we entangled logical qubits encoded in the [[7,1,3]] code with error rates 9.8 times to 500 times lower than at the physical level, and entangled logical qubits encoded in a [[12,2,4]] code based on Knill's C4/C6 scheme with error rates 4.7 times to 800 times lower than at the physical level, depending on the judicious use of post-selection
The joint team created four logical qubits using 30 of the 32 physical qubits available on the H2

milestones.claim: A Nature paper reports generating certifiably random bits on the 56-qubit Quantinuum H2-1 accessed over the Internet, certifying 71,313 bits of entropy under a restricted adversary model and additional assumptions.

evidence.quote: Here we demonstrate the generation of certifiably random bits using the 56-qubit Quantinuum H2-1 trapped-ion quantum computer accessed over the Internet.
we certify 71,313 bits of entropy under this restricted adversary and additional assumptions

milestones.claim: A peer-reviewed PRX paper reports preparing an encoded magic state in the Steane code by code switching from the fifteen-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code on H2-1; a companion preprint reports preparing magic states in a [[6,2,2]] error-detecting code on the 20-qubit H1-1 and using them for a non-Clifford controlled-Hadamard gate.

evidence.quote: Our experiment is based on the first demonstration of code switching between color codes, from the fifteen-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code to the seven-qubit Steane code. We prepare an encoded magic state in the Steane code with 82.58% probability, with an infidelity of at most
Error rate of H2-1 quantum processor is

We propose and experimentally implement a magic-state preparation protocol to fault-tolerantly prepare a pair of logical magic states in a [[6,2,2]] quantum error-detecting code using only eight physical qubits. Implementing this protocol on H1-1, a 20 qubit trapped-ion quantum processor, we prepare magic states with experimental infidelity
Today, we have published two papers

milestones.claim: A Nature paper reports using H2 to simulate digitized dynamics of the quantum Ising model, observing thermalization on timescales the authors state “severely challenge classical simulation methods”, with native partial entangler fidelities of 99.94(1)%.

evidence.quote: Here we use Quantinuum’s H2 quantum computer 9 , 10 to simulate digitized dynamics of the quantum Ising model, suppressing digitization errors well enough to observe thermalization on timescales that severely challenge classical simulation methods.
native partial entangler fidelities of 99.94(1)%

milestones.claim: Quantinuum launched Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion system using barium ions and a junction-based QCCD trap, available via cloud and on-premise; Quantinuum states 99.921% two-qubit gate fidelity.

evidence.quote: today announced the launch of Helios
Physical qubits (PQ) : 98 PQ at 99.921% 2-qubit gate fidelity, and 99.9975% 1-qubit gate fidelity.
we switched our qubits from ytterbium to barium
We report on Quantinuum Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor based on the quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture.

milestones.claim: A Quantinuum preprint reports computations on Helios in iceberg error-detecting codes and two-level concatenated iceberg codes with between 48 and 94 encoded qubits that outperform unencoded counterparts, described by the authors as “beyond break-even”; Quantinuum’s launch materials describe “94 LQ (error detected)” and “48 LQ (error corrected)”.

evidence.quote: using the 98-qubit Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor
we realize this "beyond break-even" performance with reasonable postselection rates
between 48 and 94 logical qubits
iceberg quantum error detecting (QED) and
94 LQ (error detected) globally entangled with better than physical performance
48 LQ (error corrected) with better than physical performance (99.99% state prep and measurement fidelity)

targets.statement: Quantinuum targets “universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing by 2030”, delivered by its fifth-generation system Apollo, by 2030.

evidence.quote: unveiled its roadmap to universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing by 2030
Quantinuum’s roadmap unveils its fifth-generation quantum computer, Apollo, which will be a fully fault-tolerant and universal quantum computer

targets.statement: Quantinuum targets delivery of Apollo, which it calls its “universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computer”, by 2029.

evidence.quote: positions us to fulfill our promise to deliver our universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computer, Apollo , by 2029
Apollo remains on schedule for 2029, with significant progress made across key architectural subsystems through prototyping.

targets.statement: Quantinuum targets releasing Helios with around 100 physical qubits and two-qubit gate errors below 5x10^-4 by 2025.

evidence.quote: The Quantinuum Helios™ system, which we are releasing in 2025, will offer around 100 physical qubits with two-qubit gate errors less than 5x10 -4 .

targets.statement: Quantinuum targets the launch of Sol, which it describes as its first commercially available 2D-grid-based system with hundreds of physical qubits, by 2027.

evidence.quote: Progressing towards the launch of Sol in 2027, with Sol’s trap chip back from fabrication and advancing through product validation.
After Helios we will introduce Quantinuum Sol™, our first commercially available 2D-grid-based quantum computer.
Sol will offer hundreds of physical qubits with two-qubit gate errors less than 2x10 -4

targets.statement: Quantinuum targets completing installation of a Helios system in Singapore by 2026.
